items.content:
IBP. S&OP. S&EO
Three acronyms.
One massive confusion in most organizations.
Here's the simplest way I've found to explain the difference:

S&EO = Operational level React fast. Keep operations running. Horizon: 1 to 12 weeks.
S&OP = Tactical level Balance demand and supply across all functions. Horizon: 3 to 12 months.
IBP = Strategic level Align operations with business strategy.

Drive the P&L. Horizon: 3 months to 3 years.
The higher you go, the less technical — and the more business.But here's what I always tell my clients:Your CEO doesn't care about the name. He wants to know: are we on track?
What are the 3 biggest gaps? What do we do now?That's what IBP should answer.
If yours doesn't, you're running a meeting, not a process.

Forecast Accuracy Methods: Which One Should You Use?
Choosing the right forecast accuracy metric is critical to evaluating and improving your demand planning.

Here's a breakdown of 4 standard methods:
BIAS – Simple and value-weighted, but doesn't reflect error size. It is best used as a complementary metric.
MAE (Mean Absolute Error) – Simple and relevant for most business cases. Recommended as a go-to metric.
MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error) – Common but misleading. It doesn't weigh value or error. Not recommended.
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) – Strong on error weighting but not as simple to use.

✔ Better for item-level optimization
✘ Harder to align with global logistics

items.content:
I've seen these 10 mistakes in almost every S&OP / IBP implementation I've worked on.
Some are obvious. Some are sneaky. All of them quietly kill the process.

1. No common objectives or aligned bonuses
If sales and supply chain are rewarded for different things, don't expect alignment.
2. Lack of commitment from CEO and senior management
If leadership doesn't show up, neither will anyone else, eventually.
3. Lack of clarity on responsibilities
"Who owns this decision?" should never be a mystery in the room.
4. An overly complex process
The more steps you add, the less people follow them.
5. Data not centralized or standardized
Three teams, three spreadsheets, three versions of the truth.
6. No action plan or follow-up of responsibilities
Decisions without follow-up are just nice conversations.
7. Lack of focus on essentials
If everything is a priority, nothing is.
8. Vision too short term
S&OP / IBP is not about firefighting next week. It's about steering the next 3 to 18 months.
9. Too much online, not enough human
Dashboards don't build trust. Conversations do.
10. No official S&OP / IBP process facilitator

Without a clear owner driving the process, it slowly dies on its own.
If I had to pick the one that kills the most processes: #2 and #10. Without leadership commitment and a real facilitator, everything else collapses eventually.

My Personal Story with S&OP (That Didn’t Start Well)

The very first time I heard about S&OP, I was a project manager at Decathlon.
The word was bandied about by strategy consultants... and to be honest, my first reaction was:
“It's consultant bullshit to charge more!”
But in fact, Decathlon didn't need the term S&OP to embody what it really means: collaboration, trust, and a shared culture of collective play.
(I'll talk more about the 6 pillars I identified later, for those who want to go further with me).

A few years later, I moved to Brazil, became Supply Chain Manager, took a sabbatical, landed in Australia... and joined a company through the back door as a Demand Planner.
I soon became Demand Planning Manager, then... S&OP Manager.
There he is again, that S&OP!
Our group was in the middle of a merger-acquisition with Procter & Gamble.

It was complete chaos:
👉 84 brands
👉 22 different ERPs
👉 30% turnover
👉 Extreme pressure to deliver results

I'm taking part in an S&OP training course run by our Global Vice President, a graduate of the prestigious Harvard MBA300 slides.4 hours. 
Ultra theoretical. Ultra disconnected. My head is going to explode.
What about me? I didn't even know how to extract forecasts from my 22 ERPs.
So I forgot all about it.

I went back to simple, concrete things:
👉 Visiting each member of the comex
👉 Understand their difficulties
👉 Identify one priority thing to fix quickly: a quick win.

My first executive S&OP meeting? Total chaos.
I was the first person to say publicly that we had a 22% discrepancy between product forecasts and the finance budget.
But at least...
We were finally facing reality.
And little by little, we're making progress:
👉 Teams regain confidence
👉 Tensions between departments diminished, especially with Sales and Marketing.
👉 S&OP is becoming a real management ritual
The CEO gives me his trust (and his power).
Better forecast quality, less inventory (-25%), better product availability in A and B codes (+15%). We even ended up with the best results in the group!
12 months later, I was appointed Supply Chain Director.

🌟 But this adventure has not been without pain.

I often felt alone, with little support, few people to help me in concrete terms.

If your CEO doesn't show up to your S&OP / IBP executive meetings — that's a signal.

Not about his calendar. 
About your meeting.

In my experience, there are only 3 reasons why a CEO disengages:

It's not impactful enough.
The meeting is a status update, not a decision forum. He already knows the numbers. He needs to know what to do with them.

It's not efficient. 
90 minutes of slides.10 minutes of actual decisions. That's not a meeting. That's a presentation.

It's boring. 
No tension. No real debate. Everyone agrees on everything. If there's no conflict in the room, the real conversations are happening elsewhere.

The S&OP / IBP meeting should be the place where your CEO gets clarity on three things:

Are we on track vs. business targets? What are the biggest risks and gaps? What do we need to decide — right now?
If your meeting doesn't answer those three questions in the first 20 minutes, you've lost him.
And if you've lost him, you've lost the whole process.

The Planner Roles: Who Does What in Supply Chain Planning?

In a well-structured supply chain, planners have distinct but complementary responsibilities that ensure alignment from demand forecasting to material availability.

Overview of the 4 key roles:

1. Demand Planner – Predicts future demand based on historical sales, market trends, and stakeholder inputs.
2. Supply Planner – Aligns demand, capacity, and inventory. Defines inventory targets to hit service levels.
3. Production Planner – Schedules production balances batches and constraints using ERP and capacity data.
4. Material Planner – Ensures raw materials are available when needed and monitors live stock data.

Each role contributes to ensuring product availability, optimizing stock levels, and supporting efficient operations.

Most leaders undermine themselves without realizing it.

(It happens in every email they send.)

I've coached 100s of CEOs who wonder why their emails get ignored.

The pattern is clear:

They write like they're asking for permission instead of leading.

Here’s how weak leaders communicate:

❌ "Let me know if this works for you..."
❌ "I think there might be an issue..."
❌ "Hope this email finds you well..."
❌ "I was just wondering if maybe..."
❌ "Whenever you get a chance..."
❌ "Just following up again..."
❌ "Does that make sense?"
❌ "Sorry to bother you..."
❌ "I'll try to get it done..."
❌ "I'm no expert, but..."
❌ "Sorry for the delay!"
❌ "I hate to ask, but..."

These phrases scream uncertainty.

They make recipients think your message isn't worth their time.

Great leaders write differently:

✅ "I need your help with this."
✅ "I'll have this to you by 3pm."
✅ "Can you confirm by Friday?"
✅ "Thank you for your patience."
✅ "I need your expertise on this."
✅ "Have you had time to review?"
✅ "What questions do you have?"
✅ "This needs attention by [date]."
✅ "I've identified a problem with..."
✅ "Hi Sarah, I'm reaching out about..."
✅ "Based on the data, I recommend..."
✅ "Please confirm you can meet this deadline."

Notice the difference?

Clear expectations. 
Direct language. 
Zero apologies.

This isn't about being harsh.
It's about being clear.

When you water down your language, people assume:

Your request isn't important.
You're not confident in your ask.
They can deprioritize your email.

But when you write with conviction:

People respond faster
Decisions happen quicker
Your ideas carry more weight

The most successful leaders I know don't write longer emails.
They write clearer ones.

They don't use more words.
They use better ones.

Your communication style is your leadership brand.
And every weak phrase dilutes it.

So starting today, lead with clarity.

Write like the leader you are.

Watch how quickly things change.

items.content:
I dreaded negotiations early in my career.

Then I realized:

You don’t have to be confrontational
to be a strong negotiator.

All it takes is using the right frameworks.

Here are 5 proven approaches to negotiate
every deal more effectively:

🤝 The 4 Phases Framework
(h/t: Roy Lewicki)

Great negotiators don’t jump straight to bargaining. 
They follow a structured process:

• Preparation (lay the groundwork)
• Information Exchange (build mutual understanding)
• Bargaining (explore potential solutions)
• Commitment (secure the agreement)

💪 The BATNA Strategy
(h/t: Roger Fisher & William Ury)

Your power in any negotiation comes from knowing 
your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement (BATNA).

It’s your safety net, your source of confidence. 
Always define it before you start.

🎯 The Negotiation Matrix
(h/t: Lewicki & Hiam)

Different situations call for different strategies:

• High stakes? Compete.
• Building a long-term relationship? Collaborate.
• Minor issue? Avoidance might be best.
• The relationship is too critical? Accommodate.
• Both matter equally? Compromise.

🤔 The Harvard Principled Negotiation Method
(h/t: Fisher, Ury & Patton)

This is a game-changer:
Focus on interests, not positions.

Instead of asking what they want, ask why they want it.

That’s where real value creation happens.

🎯 The ZOPA Framework
(h/t: Fisher & Ury)

The Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA) is where deals get made.

Understanding both sides’ limits helps you identify common ground. 

Everything else? It's just noise.

Key takeaway:

The best deals happen when both sides feel heard.

And the most successful negotiators aren’t the most aggressive.

They’re simply the most prepared.

items.content:
A Stanford study tracked 30,000 adults over eight years.

People under high stress had a 43% higher risk of dying.

But only if they believed stress was harmful.

The ones who saw stress as useful? No increased risk at all.

Same pressure. Different response. Different outcome.

That finding changed how Dr. Christian Poensgen and I think about performance.

The goal was never to remove stress. Stress is a fact of life.

Instead, you learn to stop the good kind from tipping into the bad.

8 ways to make that shift:

1/ ACUTE VS. CHRONIC STRESS
→ Acute stress sharpens focus and settles fast
→ Chronic stress scatters it and stays on
→ The difference is duration and recovery

2/ THE STRESS-IS-ENHANCING MINDSET (h/t Alia Crum)
→ Notice the stress, welcome it, then channel it
→ Your beliefs about stress actually change its biology

3/ THE SYNERGISTIC MINDSET (h/t David Yeager)
→ Growth mindset alone stalls at the first failure
→ Pair it with a stress-is-fuel mindset and both compound

4/ STRESS VS. ANXIETY
→ Stress has a clear trigger and a built-in off-ramp
→ Anxiety is diffuse, future-focused, and lingers without resolution

5/ SET STRESS GOALS (h/t Kelly McGonigal)
→ Avoiding stress shrinks your life
→ Pick 3 ambitious goals a year that are hard on purpose

6/ MINE YOUR PAST WINS
→ 82% of adults draw on past wins to face new stress
→ Spend 15 minutes writing about a win you had to fight for

7/ OSCILLATE, DON'T FLATLINE (h/t Loehr & Schwartz)
→ Constant output climbs, then collapses
→ Sprint and recover. That's what sustainable performance looks like

8/ TRACK YOUR HRV
→ Heart rate variability measures your stress-rest flexibility
→ High HRV shifts gears cleanly. Low HRV means you're stuck in high gear

items.content:
I used to wear 14-hour days like a badge of honor.

I thought rest was what you did after the work was done.

It took years to learn that rest is part of the work.

Your body needs seven different types of breaks.

Each one has a specific window where it works best.

Skip them and the hours keep going but the output drops.

7 breaks that protect your performance:

1/ THE MICRO-REST
→ Focus fades after 60 to 90 minutes of deep work
→ That dip is a signal, not a failure
→ Step away before it hits. Look at the horizon. Walk for 10 to 20 minutes

2/ THE BREATHING RESET
→ When stress spikes mid-task, you may not have 10 minutes
→ One breathing cycle takes about 10 seconds
→ Long inhale through the nose, short second inhale, long exhale

3/ THE POWER BREAK
→ The afternoon slump is real and predictable
→ A 10 to 20 minute nap or eyes-closed rest gives you a second wind
→ Finish well before evening so night sleep stays intact

4/ THE LUNCH BREAK
→ Midday is your best shot at a true reset
→ Eat away from your desk, leave your phone behind
→ Skip the work talk for 30 to 60 minutes

5/ THE SHUTDOWN RITUAL
→ A workday without a clear ending never really ends
→ Signal "work is over" the same way each day
→ Phone away for the evening. Takes 10 to 15 minutes

6/ THE WEEKEND RECOVERY
→ Not all time off restores you
→ Real recovery means stepping fully out of work mode
→ Spend time in nature, build a skill, take one full day off screens

7/ THE STRATEGIC VACATION
→ Recovery follows a curve. It peaks around day 7, then fades
→ Frequent planned breaks beat one long trip you save up for
→ Take one week off every three months. Book it non-refundable

Three out of four people experience burnout at work.

Most of them think the answer is pushing through.

The answer is better breaks, taken on purpose.

items.content:
Stop wasting energy on the wrong people.

Focus on the ones who WANT to grow.

After coaching 650+ CEOs, I keep seeing the same pattern.

The leaders with the strongest teams refuse to manage everyone the same way. They diagnose each person individually and adjust their approach to fit.

One of the simplest tools for this is the Skill/Will Matrix, created by Max Landsberg.

It plots every team member on two axes: skill (their ability and experience) and will (their motivation and drive).

The result is four very different types of people, each needing a very different leadership response.

🟡 Top Performers sit in the high-skill, high-will quadrant. They deliver, they push themselves, and they raise the bar for everyone around them.

These are the people you build the future of the company around. Give them ownership. Ask for their input. Raise expectations over time. Recognize them often.

The mistake is overloading them just because they can handle it. Stretch them, but invest in them too.

🟢 High Potentials have the will but not yet the skill. They are eager, hungry, and ready to grow. They just need reps.

Coach them. Break their work into small wins. Celebrate progress over perfection. Pair them with a mentor. These are your future Top Performers if you develop them well.

🔵 Disengaged Experts are the trickiest group. They have the skill, but the motivation has gone. They might be bored, burnt out, or quietly outgrowing the role.

Ask what's behind the disconnect. Reconnect them to the mission. Adjust their goals or responsibilities. Set a clear timeline for change. If nothing changes, you have your answer.

🔴 Low Performers drain energy from the rest of the team. They lack the skill and the drive to build it.

Set clear expectations, give one chance to improve, and exit respectfully if nothing changes. Keeping them in place tells everyone else that your standards are negotiable.

People will not always fit neatly into one box, and skill and will both shift over time.

The point of the matrix is to lead each person according to where they are right now. That's where your energy compounds.

items.content:
Every CEO faces the same impossible choice
(but few admit it out loud):

Step back too far → things fall apart.
Step in too close → people stop trying.

That’s the leadership paradox.

Micromanage too much?

- Your team stops thinking
- Creativity dies
- You become the bottleneck
- Burnout follows

Trust too much?

- Goals get fuzzy
- No one owns the outcome
- Deadlines slip
- Accountability fades

Both mistakes come from the same place:
Caring about the work.

The answer isn't picking a side.
It's mastering the middle.

Effective delegation looks like this:

✓ Clear goals (not vague hopes)
✓ Defined roles (with room to decide)
✓ Regular check-ins (not hovering)
✓ Support when needed
✓ Two-way feedback
✓ Accountability that sticks

This is how great leaders build teams that run without them (but not away from them).

They don't disappear.
They don't suffocate.
They lead with clarity, trust, and rhythm.

The best leaders don't choose between control and freedom.
They create structure that enables both.

If you’re scaling a team or building a business, you’ll face this paradox every day.

Master the middle.
Your team (and your sanity) will thank you.

If you had to pick, which is harder: stepping back or stepping in?

items.content:
Most companies are bleeding cash in 4 spots.

(And don't even know which wound to fix first.)

The brutal reality:

Every dollar leaving your business falls into one of these buckets:

OPERATIONS (OpEx) - The Daily Bleed
↳ Your rent, salaries, software subscriptions
↳ The money that vanishes every month
↳ Cut too deep? Your business stops tomorrow

ASSETS (CapEx) - The Big Bets
↳ That $50K machine, new warehouse, custom software
↳ Spend once, use for years
↳ Get it wrong? You're stuck with expensive mistakes

SALES (RevEx) - The Revenue Tax
↳ Every sale costs you something
↳ Materials, commissions, shipping, processing fees
↳ Ignore this? Profit margins turn into losses

MONEY (FinEx) - The Hidden Killer
↳ Interest on loans, bank fees, credit charges
↳ The cost of using other people's money
↳ Let it grow? It eats your profits alive

Let's look at 2 examples:

Coffee Shop Reality:
• OpEx: $15K/month (rent, barista wages, utilities)
• CapEx: $80K once (espresso machine, renovation)
• RevEx: $3 per cup sold (beans, cup, lid)
• FinEx: $500/month (equipment loan interest)

SaaS Startup Truth:
• OpEx: $50K/month (team, AWS, office)
• CapEx: $200K once (custom platform build)
• RevEx: $20 per customer (payment fees, onboarding)
• FinEx: $2K/month (venture debt interest)

Most founders lump all expenses together.
Then wonder why they can't scale.

But when you separate them?

OpEx → Find your true burn rate
CapEx → Time investments perfectly
RevEx → Price products profitably
FinEx → Optimize capital structure

Crucial insights:

✓ High OpEx? You're not scalable yet
✓ No CapEx? You're not building moats
✓ Rising RevEx? Your unit economics are broken
✓ Climbing FinEx? You're overleveraged

Common traps:

❌ Treating CapEx like OpEx (and vice versa)
❌ Ignoring RevEx when setting prices
❌ Letting FinEx compound silently
❌ Not tracking any of them separately

Watch what happens when you finally see where your money really goes.

Your future self will thank you.
Your investors will respect you.
Your business will actually scale.

Stop managing "expenses."
Start managing OpEx, CapEx, RevEx, and FinEx.

That's how you build something that lasts.

items.content:
I used to schedule my hardest work first thing in the morning. For years I thought that was discipline. It was a guess.

When Dr. Christian Poensgen and I started writing Ultraproductive, we dug into the research on chronotypes.

Turns out you're born one of three types:
A Lark, a Third Bird, or an Owl.

Each one has a different peak window for deep focus.

And most people have no idea which one they are.

1/ LARKS (14% OF PEOPLE)
→ Peak hits 30 minutes after waking
→ Your sharpest hours come before most people open their inbox

2/ THIRD BIRDS (65% OF PEOPLE)
→ Peak hits about 3 hours after waking
→ Mid-morning is your golden zone for demanding work

3/ OWLS (21% OF PEOPLE)
→ Peak hits 11 hours after waking
→ Your deepest focus arrives in the late afternoon or evening

Each type also has a day shape, a signature strength, and a pitfall.

If you feel like you can never concentrate, it might not be a focus problem. You might just be scheduling your hardest work at your worst time.

Match your peak window to your most important tasks.

The hours stay the same. The output changes.
